terms.gloss: a feature, a characteristic: what belongs to someone or something in particular
terms.grammar: noun, second declension (the neuter of proprius); usually proprium est with a genitive
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.17: proprium hoc statuō esse virtūtis, conciliāre animōs hominum
Caes. BG 6.23: hoc proprium virtūtis exīstimant
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “a characteristic mark, a sign, characteristic”. The genitive alone can say the same: cujusvīs hominis est errāre, it is in any man’s nature to err (Cic. Phil. 12.5).

terms.grammar: phrase: habeō with hoc, and an ut-clause saying what the feature is
evidence: Cic. Pis. 81: habet hoc virtūs … ut virōs fortīs speciēs ejus et pulchritūdō etiam in hoste posita dēlectet

phrases.latin: proprium hoc statuō esse virtūtis, conciliāre animōs hominum et ad ūsūs suōs adjungere
phrases.english: I hold this to be the mark of virtue: to win people’s hearts and attach them to one’s own service

phrases.latin: Habet hoc virtūs, quam tū nē dē faciē quidem nōstī, ut virōs fortīs speciēs ejus et pulchritūdō etiam in hoste posita dēlectet.
phrases.english: Virtue, which you do not know even by sight, has this about it: brave men are delighted by its look and beauty even in an enemy.
Any man may make a mistake

sources: Lewis & Short: proprius · Lewis & Short: habeo
Cicero, De officiis 2, In Pisonem and Philippics 12, and Caesar, Bellum Gallicum 6, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (9 November 2026).
